title: Théorie des cycles algébriques : conjectures de Hodge, Tate, Lefschetz, Weil : notes manuscrites (s.d.), lettre (1965).

deep.reconstruction:
This is the first page of Grothendieck's letter to Serre dated 27 August 1965. It is the letter in which he first states what became the 'standard conjectures', and it is published in the Grothendieck–Serre Correspondence (SMF 2001; English edition AMS 2004).

Setting:
- X is a smooth connected projective variety of dimension n over an algebraically closed field k.
- Y is a smooth hyperplane section of X.
- C^i(X) is the group of codimension-i cycles modulo algebraic equivalence, tensored with Q.
- ξ ∈ C^1(X) is the class of Y.

Conjecture A (the Lefschetz-type standard conjecture, stated 'purely geometrically'): for 2i ≤ n, cup product with ξ^{n-2i} gives an isomorphism C^i(X) → C^{n-i}(X).

Grothendieck adds three remarks:
1. Modulo unchecked details, it would suffice to prove surjectivity, and only in the case n = 2i+1. The first open case is i=1, n=3: divisors versus curves on a threefold.
2. A implies the cycle analogues of the Lefschetz comparison theorems between X and Y, via direct and inverse image (with C^i playing the role of H^{2i}).
3. A also implies cohomological hard Lefschetz, ξ^{n-i}: H^i ≅ H^{2n-i} with Q_ℓ coefficients, which he stresses was then unproved.

What was proved was only weak Lefschetz, coming from the cohomological dimension of the affine variety U = X − Y being ≤ n:
- H^i(X) → H^i(Y) is bijective for i ≤ n−2 and injective for i = n−1;
- dually, the Gysin map H^i(Y) → H^{i+2}(X) is bijective for i ≥ n and surjective for i = n−1.

The purpose is a cohomology-free formulation for Serre of the key conjectures that would give the Weil conjectures and a usable notion of motive. The next page continues with A' (a weak-Lefschetz surjectivity C^i(Y) → C^{i+1}(X)), the Künneth consequence, and Conjecture B (Hodge-index positivity on primitive cycles).
errors: Conjecture A as stated, modulo algebraic equivalence with Q-coefficients, is false. Griffiths (1969) showed that homological and algebraic equivalence differ for curves on general quintic threefolds. Clemens (1983) showed the Griffiths group can have infinite rank. So for i=1, n=3 (exactly the case Grothendieck flags as 'the first that escapes'), C^1(X) = NS(X)⊗Q is finite-dimensional while C^2(X) can be infinite-dimensional, and surjectivity fails. Grothendieck already hedges on the next page, suggesting A might need to be stated for cohomological equivalence. The modern Lefschetz standard conjecture B(X) is formulated for homological or numerical equivalence.

Relatedly, the claims on the following page that B implies τ-equivalence = numerical equivalence and finite-dimensionality of C^m are false for algebraic equivalence, for the same Griffiths reason. This is noted in the editorial comments of the published Correspondence.
The weak Lefschetz statements on this page are correct as stated. The hard Lefschetz theorem for ℓ-adic cohomology was later proved by Deligne (Weil II, 1980) without the standard conjectures.

Cohomological hard Lefschetz with Q_ℓ coefficients (then open)

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known, published 1965 letter introducing the standard conjectures. Its contents, including the overly strong algebraic-equivalence formulation later refuted by Griffiths, are fully documented in the Grothendieck–Serre Correspondence and its notes.
transcription_corrections: The inequality in Conjecture A appears typed as '2i <' with a mark beneath, i.e. '≤'. The transcription's 2i ≤ n is mathematically the right reading.
The coefficients written 'Q_ℓ' appear as an underlined Q with a handwritten ℓ; the transcription is fine.
